This post’s R-trick: %<>%
When programming within the Tidyverse, we often use the pipe operator (%>%) that allows us to write efficient pipelines. To assign the output of that pipeline to some object, we often use the structure
data <- data %>% pipeline
%>% is defined in {magrittr} and imported by the Tidyverse. However, if we import {magrittr}, we also get access to %<>%. This is a useful pipe, as it summarises the above structure:
data %<>% pipeline
It’s a nice shorthand and looks cool. Happy coding!

title: Het promotieonderzoek van Roemer
text:

title: Going to the ERA congress 2026
text:
Hullo again!
A week ago, we wrapped up the 63rd European Renal Association congres in Glasgow. We look back at a succesful midweek in which we were able to connect with colleagues, held interesting discussions in regards to our research, and were visible from the main stage to the research zone.
Looking back, we not only shared interesting insights from our work, but also were able to catch up in person with our collaborators and plant the seeds of promising new collaborations.

This post’s R-trick: ->
One of the basic operators of R is <-, the object assignment operator. Although not best practice, you can also flexibly use -> instead. This is sometimes helpful if you are working from the console instead of from a script, and want to quickly store some output. Instead of going to the start of the code (or pipeline) and appending the object operator there, you can just keep on writing:
data %>% filter(!indicator) -> dat_check
Happy coding!

title: De nier-data onderzoeksgroep van het UMC Utrecht
text:
Welkom op de blog van U-KREAT. Wij zijn de nier-data onderzoeksgroep van het UMC Utrecht. Leuk dat u meeleest.
Hier vindt u informatie over ons team en de projecten waar we mee bezig zijn. We begrijpen dat die Engelse informatie niet altijd makkelijk te begrijpen is, doordat het is geschreven voor andere onderzoekers. Daarom hebben we ook deze blog.
Op deze blog delen wij interessante informatie in begrijpbaar Nederlands, zoals dit bericht. Dit soort berichten staan onder het kopje ‘In begrijpbare taal’.

title: The UMC Utrecht NE group: An introduction
text:
Welcome to the blog of the Utrecht Kidney Research & Epidemiological Analyses Team (U-KREAT) at the UMC Utrecht! Here, we will share interesting publications (both from our own group and from other researchers), give updates on conferences we attended, and share posts aimed at laymen (written in understandable Dutch).
To kick things off, today, we had our first get together at the Café Creatinine. Although our group has existed for a longer time, this was given shape in an informal manner. Today marks the first occurrence of our biweekly recurring meeting. These meetings will serve not only as a short moment to connect with each other, but also to discuss currently ongoing projects, discuss articles, give talks, host external speakers, etc.
…
To finish off, I’ll append an R trick to each post (until I run out of tricks)

This post’s R-trick: multicursor
Did you know you can activate a multicursor in R? This allows you to write the same code on multiple lines simultaneously. Great for if you are writing code in bulk! To activate it, simply hold the Alt/Option key and drag the cursor along the lines that you want the cursor to apply to. On some operating systems, you may need to press the Alt/Option key one more time to activate the cursor. Happy bulk-writing!
